title: Time Reflection-Refraction Crossover at Topological Kramers Edge States
abstract: Time-reversal symmetry protects helical edge states against static nonmagnetic backscattering. We show that spatially uniform temporal modulation produces a time reflection-refraction crossover within the same quantum spin Hall phase while preserving time-reversal symmetry of the instantaneous Hamiltonian. A finite gap to the bulk and an edge splitting that vanishes at the Kramers crossing allow the modulation to suppress bulk excitation while remaining nonadiabatic between the edge channels. Virtual transitions through bulk states enable coherent conversion between counter-propagating edge channels at fixed crystal momentum. Near the crossing, $qT$ governs the leading crossover dynamics for a fixed ramp shape, where $q$ is the momentum offset and $T$ the ramp duration. Coherent interference can suppress and restore reflection as the ramp slows. In the adiabatic limit, two initially time-reversed wave packets follow their respective propagation branches and acquire equal geometric displacements. Their group-velocity contributions cancel, isolating the contribution from the Berry curvature to be directly observable. Temporal modulation thus controls protected states and quantum geometry along a topological edge.
summary: This paper theoretically examines how time-dependent modulation controls transport at topological Kramers edge states, leading to a crossover between time reflection and time refraction. By analyzing the edge subspace dynamics, the authors show that the process is governed by the product of momentum offset and ramp time ($qT$). This work demonstrates that temporal control can isolate and measure the geometric contribution of the Berry curvature in these protected quantum channels.
main_problem: The paper investigates the crossover between time reflection and time refraction phenomena at topological Kramers edge states when subjected to time-dependent modulation.
main_result: Temporal modulation allows for controlled time reflection/refraction even when time-reversal symmetry is preserved, and the adiabatic limit isolates the Berry curvature contribution to the geometric displacement.
method: The analysis uses effective Schrödinger equations for the edge subspace, employing covariant derivatives and analyzing the evolution in a parallel frame to derive scaling laws based on the product of momentum offset and ramp duration (qT).
model_or_system: The system is modeled using Quantum Spin Hall (QSH) edge states, analyzed via an effective Hamiltonian that couples the edge doublet to the bulk spectrum. The dynamics are controlled by a time-dependent parameter that drives the system through a Kramers crossing.
key_observables: Reflection probability (R), Refraction probability (T), physical geometric displacement ($\Delta X_K$), and the scaling dependence on $qT$.
important_parameters: The crossover dynamics are governed by the product $qT$, the finite bulk gap ($\Delta_b$), and the vanishing edge splitting ($\Delta_e(q)$) at the crossing.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a finite bulk gap, allowing the edge subspace to track the control, and utilizes approximations to decouple the edge dynamics from the bulk continuum.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate temporal scattering, contrasting forbidden static backscattering with allowed time reflection. They also show the dependence of reflection on $qT$ and the convergence of the physical pair midpoint to the geometric limit in the adiabatic regime.
paper_structure: The paper develops the dynamics by projecting the full Hamiltonian onto the edge subspace, deriving the evolution equation in the parallel frame, analyzing the resulting coupled differential equations for branch amplitudes, and finally calculating the geometric displacement in the adiabatic limit.
why_interesting: The work provides a detailed theoretical framework for controlling topological edge states using time-dependent driving, which is highly relevant for understanding coherent quantum transport in engineered superconducting or topological materials.
